prize_parts.citation: for credibly identified empirical evidence on how technology and import competition reshape labour demand, wages and local labour-market adjustment

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged from round 1: B037 with Autor, Dorn and Hanson. The chair asks for one sentence on what the discovery is. Mine is that technology and import competition shift the demand for labour, and the adjustment is local, slow and uneven, as shown by designs that others could re-run and challenge. The test I weight most is whether the central claims are exposed to scrutiny and survive it. For the import-shock evidence they have. The shift-share designs, pre-trend checks and persistence results have been re-examined many times, and the qualitative pattern has reappeared in data from other countries. Debate over magnitudes is what a mature programme looks like, and it is not a sign the work is premature. Autor carries both the task and technology evidence and the import-shock evidence. That is why the citation can speak about technology without naming a fourth person or claiming the whole task literature. Dorn is a core co-author of the import-shock papers. Leaving him out would misstate where the most replicable evidence came from. My reasoning on Dorn versus Katz has shifted during this round. I now think the overlap with the 2023 prize is more thematic than substantive, and I no longer treat it as my main reason. I prefer Dorn because the credited discovery is then the one body of design-based evidence, jointly authored and widely re-tested, and the citation can be worded to match it.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is still that B037 joins two strands that could be judged separate discoveries: the skill-premium and task framework, and the import-shock evidence. My trio credits the second strand directly and the first only through Autor. If the Committee judges the framework to be the main discovery, Katz's omission, and the absence of Levy, Murnane and Acemoglu (already a laureate), under-credits it. The size and persistence of the China-shock effects, and the sensitivity of some estimates to specification and the shift-share instrument, remain contested. I have not re-checked the underlying papers and rely on my recollection of the literature. Adjacency to the 2023 and 2024 prizes on labour-market history, skills and institutions could also lower the weight a majority gives it. Finally, my own opening ranked B008 first and B037 third. A member who weights replication this heavily should say openly that the choice between a clean two-name trade-theory prize and a composite three-name labour prize is a close judgement.

responses.point: Fredriksson keeps Katz because the achievement is about technology and trade together and Katz-Murphy and Autor-Katz-Krueger supply the skill-premium framing. He argues a Dorn trio narrows the prize to the China shock, which has the more contested interpretation. He accepts Autor and Hanson alone as a fallback and would not oppose the trade-shock trio on scientific grounds.
responses.response: I accept that the Katz variant is the broader prize and that his reading is coherent. I do not agree that the Dorn trio drops the technology side. Autor is central to both the task evidence and the import-shock evidence, and the citation says technology explicitly. On the contested interpretation, a narrower claim about credibly identified adjustment evidence is easier to defend than a broader claim about the whole skill-premium story. I would also move away from my opening two-name Autor and Hanson idea. It would leave out a core author of the strand whose replicability I value most. I would take it only if the Committee cannot settle a third name, and I note that he regards it as a fallback too.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson argues that the 2023 prize cited women's labour-market outcomes over time and the 2024 prize cited institutions and prosperity, so neither covers the demand-side account of how technology and trade reallocate labour. She would word the citation around the combined technology and trade-adjustment evidence, not a claim to originate the task model.
responses.response: This answers the chair's overlap question in part, and it changed my reasoning. I now agree the overlap with 2023 is mostly thematic, and I withdraw the line from round 1 that it was my main reason for preferring Dorn. My remaining case is attribution coherence. Her proposed wording is close to mine and I adopt its restraint. I still read the two strands as less unified than she does. The identification strategies differ, so I would not let the citation imply a single originating model. Where we differ now is only the third name, and I agree with her that the Committee should settle that on attribution grounds, not by default.

responses.point: Hassler, the chair, moved to Autor, Dorn and Hanson. His citation is the narrowest ('empirical analysis'), tied to the import-shock papers with Autor carrying the task strand, and he accepts that persistence is debated and that dropping Katz leaves out the education-versus-technology framing.
responses.response: I share his trio and his reason for adopting it. His candour about the cost of leaving out the long-run education-technology framing is what I would want written into the Committee's record. I would keep my citation slightly fuller than his, naming technology as well as import competition, because Autor's work legitimately supports that. I am not claiming that two members agreeing on Dorn is evidence of merit. The point is that we reached the same attribution from two routes: his overlap argument and my replicability argument.

responses.point: Friberg prefers B022. He says the BLP methods changed what can be credibly measured and that his argument weakens if the Committee wants a prize tied to a specific empirical finding. He would not argue that B022 should outrank a candidate with a clear substantive result. He also treats B037 as possibly two bundled strands and keeps it as an alternative.
responses.response: I appreciate how clearly he states the limit of his case. On my own criteria B022 is a serious candidate, because the methods have been used and stress-tested by many groups for about thirty years, and I have not found a reason to doubt that. What keeps B037 ahead for me is that its main claims are about economic outcomes and are exposed to direct re-testing. A method is checked by its use, whereas this evidence is checked against data that others can re-estimate. His bundling concern is the same one I list against my own preference. I would settle it by wording the citation around the import-shock and technology adjustment evidence, which is the narrow-core reading he favours. I would not call B022 weaker on merit.

responses.point: Krusell argues for Kiyotaki and Moore (B025) as a clean two-name mechanism, but accepts that the evidence for collateral-driven amplification rests mainly on stylised and calibrated models and that the size of the effect depends on calibration. He also says his own field's priors may bias his view.
responses.response: The chair asked whether anyone can cite direct evidence for the collateral channel beyond the post-2008 narrative. Krusell does not do so, and he concedes that quantitative amplification is contested, so my round-1 concern stands. I would also separate relevance from confirmation. The mechanism clearly organised thinking after 2008, but a crisis narrative is one episode and the specific amplification claim is not directly tested by it. I agree his attribution is cleaner than mine. I do not treat that as a reason to move B025 into my configuration, and my view would change only if someone points to credible, direct tests of the collateral channel.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee treats the technology and task strand and the import-shock strand as one discovery or two. I read them as closely related but separately identified, and have not resolved it.
Whether Dorn or Katz is the better third name. My preference rests on attribution coherence for the replicable evidence, and I accept the Katz variant is the broader prize.

How large and persistent the China-shock effects are, and how robust shift-share designs and task measures are. I rely on my recollection of the literature and have not checked the papers independently.
Whether adjacency to the 2023 and 2024 prizes should lower the weight of B037, a risk that I and several colleagues acknowledge.

Whether B008 should take priority if the Committee prefers a clean two-name trade-theory prize, given that Helpman also appears on B004 and could be credited only once, and that the empirical origins of the field have claimants outside the credited names.
Whether the B013 framework can be attributed to three people without arbitrary exclusions.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from my supplied profile with respect to Autor, Dorn, Hanson, Katz or the credited names on B008 and B013. I have no co-authorship or institutional tie to them. Disclosed for transparency only: I am at the Stockholm School of Economics, where other committee members are also affiliated (Andersson has disclosed an SSE affiliation). I co-authored in 2009 with Tore Ellingsen, an SSE colleague and former committee chair, and my main co-author Magnus Johannesson is a former committee member. None of these is a candidate connection. My metascience background may lead me to give more weight to replicability and robustness than other members do. That is a perspective, not a conflict. All of this is disclosed, not adjudicated.
